In 1975, the combined cooperatives net generating capacity was 125,000 kW and 33,000 kW was purchased from Central Power and Light Company. The required reserve capacity was 15% of 123,000 kW or 18,500 kW, leaving a net assured capacity of 104,500 kW. The combined cooperative system's peak demand in 1975 occurred on August 21st at 7:00 p.m., and was 131,370 kW.
The South Texas Electric Co-op owns a 48.0 MW gas and oil steam turbine plant which is part of the above listed 125.0 MW of net generating capacity. It plans to construct a 400.0 MW lignite-fired steam turbine unit scheduled for service in July 1980, and another 400.0 MW lignite-fired unit is to be added in June 1981. These lignite plants will be a joint venture between two other co-ops, the Medina Co-op, and Brazos Electric Co-op. The cooperative also plans to contract for the 57.0 MW of Amistad power.
2.69 From the foregoing, it is clear that Amistad hydropower would provide only a very small part of the power over the large service area to which it would be connected, i.e., the combine intertied CP&L, Medina, and South Texas Co-op networks. But its geographic location is strategic so that it can produce power to greatly reduce line losses. When used to serve a peaking demand, which is what the Amistad plant will mainly serve, it will compliment the new lignite-fired plants in such a way as to save considerable fuel.
Expected Changes in the Environmental Setting in the Absence of the Proposed Action
2.70 Certain elements of the natural landscape (e.g., topography, physiography, and geology) within the Rio Grande floodplain are not expected to change significantly over the next 50 years. However, some alteration could be motivated from mining operations or from land use changes associated with rural or suburban developments.
2.71 If hydropower is not added to the existing dam, there is little doubt that consumers will obtain the power from some other source. One of two probabilities will occur. Either crude oil from foreign nations will be imported, refined, and burned to generate peaking power or lignite will be mined from open pits in south Texas, processed, and burned to maintain a steam reserve to meet the peaking demand. Of these two, the latter is the most likely. Although this will not result in a change in the physical environment immediately along the Rio Grande, it will result in higher costs for electricity to all consumers including those that live in and around the river communities.
2.72 Wildlife communities should not demonstrate any significant change without a disruption to their habitat or natural setting. The Amistad-Rio Grande-Falcon fisheries should also maintain or improve their populations. Natural weathering, flooding, and man's actions are expected to continue to have an adverse impact on archeological and historical resources. Nevertheless, future archeological investigations may salvage some of this heritage. The OBERS projections to year 2020 for the Water Resource Area 1308 (Rio Grande-Amistad) show that the population will increase about 25 percent between 1980 and 2020; employment will increase about 43 percent; total personal income will increase about 357 percent; earnings from agriculture will increase about 157 percent; earnings from contract construction will increase about 400 percent; earnings from manufacturing will increase about 328 percent; and earnings from wholesale and retail trade will increase about 336 (USWRC, 1972). Based on these projections, considerable economic expansion and social and cultural changes can be expected in this study area.
